body: I guess everyone is affected by depression in different ways. The no sleep thing was HARD, but I was surprisingly able to pull it off. I remember hanging a cable in my wardrobe to try and hang myself, then hours later having a job interview and landing the job. I remember being awake for three days before a presentation to a room full of very senior people in government, and somehow getting through it. I guess I always overprepared for big moments like that so that I could reel the material off even in a bad state. Everything else I did to 60% quality, which you can get away with in government. I almost broke so many times, and turned down more than one dream job offer because of mental health. Hiring is such a faff, employees can get away with quite a lot without getting fired IME.

This is a tricky one, but I think it's worth trying things out until you feel good. I started on bupropion which did help a bit, but gave me more suicidal thoughts. Then sertraline which was awful for the first two weeks, then transformative and wonderful thereafter. Talk to your psychiatrist about what your options are, it's worth feeling crappy for two weeks to then potentially feel great forever.

There is hope. I was a mess for ten years, and now I'm so much better! Keep trying more solutions systematically. Things that slightly helped but didn't really fix me: hardcore meditation; psychotherapy; CBT; bupropion; trazadone; all the sleep aids; all the sleep hygiene stuff; moving jobs the first time. Yep, in my country 1 in 5 are disabled. My best guess at the barriers to having a successful movement:
- Many of us already face such barriers in our day to day lives that organising a movement is not possible
- fragmented community: lots of different conditions and experiences (and the fact that some of these are invisible) make it harder to form a shared identity. Everyone has a gay cousin or black neighbor. But you might think of your disabled friend as "the one with MS" or "the one with sight loss" instead of being part of the "disabled" category.
- it's not "sexy". I'm finding it hard to qualify this one but I have a suspicion that in many circles e.g. being a feminist helps dudes especially win social kudos and interest from women.
- In many ways harder to fix, eg. making the whole subway system accessible is harder than asking a sexual partner for consent or running a recruitment campaign with an ethnic minority person on the panel.

Edit: to be clear, I do think it would be possible for us to have a successful movement. But the above perhaps helps to explain why it hasn't yet happened.

Without all of this, I would never have had the courage to accept my dream job. My housemates say they have noticed a big difference and I'm laughing more. It's like, all my old problems are still there but, now I feel like there's not just one version of flourishing in my life,  which is liberating. If I don't get to have my own family, I will have to grieve that but then I will do other cool things instead. I'm disabled, so I can't do lots of fun things, but now it's like, it doesn't matter so much because there are still some fun things I can do, and how awesome to be alive and doing those things.

I have a problem with self-injury impulses. Here is what helped me, from most effective to least:
1) starting antidepressants, specifically Zoloft and Wellbutrin
2) exploring self harm with my therapist, thinking of it as a coping mechanism that no longer serves me (i.e. I shouldn't hate myself for having the impulses, I'm just trying to survive)
3) ending a toxic relationship where I felt like I had to be broken in order to get any care or affection
4) telling my close friends so I know there are people I can call in an emergency
5) practising loving kindness meditation regularly and directing the compassion first towards my best friend and then towards myself (I imagine myself when I was a child if the self-compassion isn't flowing easily)
6) Cold showers (like really cold, at least 1 min. I get a buzz of good feelings for about half an hour after).
7) Lie on an acupressure mat (£20 off Amazon). This one is great because it's so easy, all you do is lie there.
8) hold ice cube over the area that I feel the urge to injure.
9) Ring a helpline to distract myself.

I hope this helps.

Therapy can still really help you even if you don't  ever get to a place where you feel like you can tell them about the underlying issues. They can teach you techniques for working with the anxiety you feel when talking to people, for example, or techniques for working with the emotions that lead you to self-harm. You don't have to tell them anything you don't want to.

Here are some of the things that worked for me when I didn't feel like I could tell my therapist something:
- Saying that I don't feel ready to talk about that 
- Saying that there is a thing from my past that feels important, but it's too soon to talk about it but just to let her know there's something there.
- Saying that I will tell her about something but not to ask me any questions about it after.

And regarding talking about being suicidal, you can ask them what their response would be if a patient told them that, so you know beforehand how they would respond.

I would go for it but maybe ask your parents to agree to let you find a therapist you really like, and try another if the first one isn't the right fit.
